title: Enterprise patch management as routine maintenance
guidance: Treat patching as planned, recurring maintenance rather than emergency work. Keep an inventory of what runs where, group assets by how much disruption they tolerate, and give each group a regular update window plus a faster path for urgent fixes. Decide the response to each vulnerability: patch, mitigate with another control until a patch can be applied, transfer the risk, or accept it for a stated time. Record the decision and the owner.

title: When a patch cannot be applied yet
guidance: If no fix exists or the system cannot be updated in time, reduce risk with temporary mitigations: restrict network access to the affected service, disable only the vulnerable feature if the vendor documents that workaround, add monitoring for exploitation attempts, and isolate the asset if it is internet-facing and actively exploited. Set a review date, and remove the mitigation only after the real fix is installed and verified.

title: Prioritise known exploited vulnerabilities (CISA KEV)
guidance: A CVE listed in the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog has reliable evidence of exploitation in the wild, so it should be fixed ahead of higher-scored but unexploited issues. Each entry names the required action, usually applying the vendor update or following vendor mitigations, or discontinuing the product if no fix exists. Internet-facing assets with a KEV-listed CVE deserve the shortest deadline.

title: KEV remediation deadlines (BOD 22-01)
guidance: US federal agencies must remediate KEV-listed vulnerabilities by the due date in the catalog, typically two weeks after listing for recent CVEs. Private organisations are not bound by the directive, but the same timelines are a sensible benchmark: track every KEV match on your assets with an owner and a due date, and report what is overdue.

title: Using EPSS exploit probability
guidance: EPSS estimates the probability that a CVE will be exploited in the next 30 days; the percentile shows how it ranks against all scored CVEs. Use it alongside severity, not instead of it: CVSS describes how bad exploitation would be, EPSS how likely it is. A high EPSS score on an exposed, critical asset is a strong reason to move a fix forward. Scores change daily, so re-check rather than storing them as fixed facts.

title: Reading a CVSS score and vector
guidance: CVSS base scores range from 0 to 10 and describe the intrinsic severity of a vulnerability. The vector string explains why: attack vector (network, adjacent, local, physical), attack complexity, privileges and user interaction required, and impact on confidentiality, integrity and availability. A network-reachable flaw needing no privileges or user interaction is far more urgent on an internet-facing host than on an isolated one. The base score does not include your environment, so adjust priority for exposure and asset value.

title: Decision-based prioritisation (SSVC)
guidance: SSVC prioritises a vulnerability by decisions rather than a single score: is it being exploited, is it automatable, what is the technical impact, and what is the mission and well-being impact of the affected asset. The outcome is an action level from tracking it in normal cycles up to acting immediately. It is a useful way to explain to stakeholders why one fix comes before another.

title: NVD CVSS metrics and severity ranges
guidance: NVD publishes CVSS assessments for CVEs and maps base scores to qualitative ratings: low 0.1-3.9, medium 4.0-6.9, high 7.0-8.9 and critical 9.0-10.0. NVD analysis can lag behind publication, and the vendor's own score may differ; when they disagree, read the vendor advisory for the affected versions and the fixed version.

title: Ubuntu security notices and fixed package versions
guidance: Ubuntu Security Notices (USNs) list, per release, the exact package versions that fix each CVE. Compare the installed version (apt policy <package>) with the fixed version for your release, then update with sudo apt update followed by sudo apt install --only-upgrade <package>, or apply all pending security updates. Some fixes are only in Ubuntu Pro (ESM) packages for older releases.

title: Automatic security updates on Ubuntu
guidance: The unattended-upgrades package installs security updates automatically. Enable it with sudo dpkg-reconfigure --priority=low unattended-upgrades, and check /etc/apt/apt.conf.d/50unattended-upgrades for which origins are allowed and whether automatic reboots are permitted. Logs are under /var/log/unattended-upgrades/. Keep automatic reboots off on servers that need a planned window, and watch for a pending reboot instead.

title: Pinning and downgrading Debian/Ubuntu packages
guidance: To stop a package from changing, use apt-mark hold <package> and release it later with apt-mark unhold. APT preferences (files in /etc/apt/preferences.d/) can pin a package to a specific version or origin; a pin priority above 1000 allows a downgrade. To roll back after a bad update, install the earlier version explicitly (apt install <package>=<version>) if it is still available in the archive or the local cache, then hold it until a fixed release arrives. Note that rolling back a security update reopens the vulnerability.

title: Debian security advisories and tracker
guidance: Debian publishes Debian Security Advisories (DSA) and a security tracker showing, per CVE and per release, whether a package is vulnerable and which version fixes it. Make sure the security repository for your release is in the APT sources, then apply updates with apt update and apt upgrade. A CVE marked as not affecting your release, or as a minor issue postponed, explains why no update appears.

title: Security updates on RHEL with dnf
guidance: On Red Hat Enterprise Linux, list available security errata with dnf updateinfo list --security, inspect one with dnf updateinfo info <advisory>, and install only security fixes with dnf upgrade --security, or a specific advisory with dnf upgrade --advisory=<RHSA-ID>. Red Hat backports fixes into the same upstream version number, so check the full package release string against the advisory rather than the upstream version.

source.name: Red Hat: Managing and monitoring security updates

title: Rolling back and locking packages on RHEL
guidance: dnf history lists past transactions; dnf history undo <id> reverts one, provided the earlier package versions are still available from a repository. dnf downgrade <package> installs the previous available version. To keep a package at its current version, the versionlock plugin (dnf versionlock add <package>) prevents updates until the lock is removed. Downgrading a security fix reintroduces the vulnerability, so treat it as a short, documented exception.

source.name: Red Hat: Managing software with the DNF tool

title: Restart what loads an updated library
guidance: Updating a shared library such as OpenSSL or glibc does not protect processes that already loaded the old copy. After the update, restart the services that use it, or reboot. On RHEL, dnf needs-restarting lists processes using outdated files and needs-restarting -r says whether a reboot is required. On Debian and Ubuntu, the needrestart tool reports the same, and /var/run/reboot-required appears when a reboot is needed. A kernel update always needs a reboot unless live patching is in use.

source.name: Red Hat: Managing and monitoring security updates

title: Kernel live patching on Ubuntu
guidance: Canonical Livepatch applies critical kernel security fixes without a reboot on supported Ubuntu LTS kernels. It reduces the window of exposure but does not replace regular reboots into a fully updated kernel, because not every fix can be live patched. Check status with canonical-livepatch status.

title: Checking an installed package version
guidance: Before and after a fix, confirm the installed version from the package manager rather than the application banner. On Debian and Ubuntu, apt-cache policy <package> (or apt policy) shows the installed and candidate versions, and dpkg -l <package> lists what is installed. On RHEL, rpm -q <package> shows the full version and release. Compare the result with the fixed version in the vendor advisory for your exact release.

title: Windows updates and servicing
guidance: Windows receives cumulative monthly quality updates that include all earlier security fixes, so installing the latest cumulative update for the build closes older CVEs too. Manage them centrally with Windows Update for Business, WSUS or Configuration Manager, use deployment rings so a small pilot group updates first, and confirm the OS build number afterwards. An unsupported Windows version no longer receives fixes and should be upgraded.

source.name: Microsoft Learn: Windows client updates and servicing

title: Finding the Windows update that fixes a CVE
guidance: The Microsoft Security Update Guide lists each CVE with the affected products and the KB article of the update that fixes it, plus any documented mitigations and workarounds and whether exploitation was detected. Match the product and build of the asset to the right KB, then confirm installation with Get-HotFix or the update history.

source.name: Microsoft Security Response Center Update Guide

title: Removing a Windows update that caused problems
guidance: A standalone update can be removed with wusa /uninstall /kb:<number>, or from Settings under update history. Cumulative updates that include a servicing stack update may not be removable this way; DISM /Online /Remove-Package with the package name is the documented alternative. Removing an update reopens the vulnerabilities it fixed, so pause the update only briefly and track the vendor's corrected release.

source.name: Microsoft Support: Windows Update Standalone Installer

title: Windows Defender Firewall basics
guidance: Keep Windows Firewall enabled for all profiles (domain, private, public) with inbound connections blocked by default, and add allow rules only for the programs and ports a host really serves, scoped to the source addresses that need them. Manage rules centrally through Group Policy or Intune so local changes cannot quietly open ports. Turning the firewall off to solve a connectivity problem removes protection for every port; add a narrow rule instead.

title: Creating a scoped Windows firewall rule
guidance: New-NetFirewallRule creates a rule from PowerShell. Scope each allow rule tightly: set -Direction Inbound, -Protocol and -LocalPort, and limit -RemoteAddress to the management subnet or the specific clients that need access. To block a port, create a rule with -Action Block. Test from an allowed and a non-allowed address, and remove temporary rules when the change window ends.

title: Do not switch off Microsoft Defender; use tamper protection
guidance: Attackers commonly try to disable antivirus and EDR before acting. Tamper protection stops local changes to key Defender settings such as real-time protection. If Defender flags a legitimate tool, investigate the detection and, if it is a confirmed false positive, add the narrowest possible exclusion through central management; never disable protection to make an alert go away.

title: Disabling SMBv1
guidance: SMBv1 is obsolete and was abused by worms such as WannaCry. Check whether it is in use with Get-SmbServerConfiguration | Select EnableSMB1Protocol, and disable it with Set-SmbServerConfiguration -EnableSMB1Protocol $false (or remove the SMB1 optional feature on clients). Very old devices such as some printers or NAS units may still need it; replace or isolate them rather than keeping SMBv1 on for everyone.

source.name: Microsoft Learn: Detect, enable and disable SMBv1, SMBv2 and SMBv3

title: Securing SMB traffic and port 445
guidance: SMB on TCP 445 should never be reachable from the internet; block it at the perimeter. Inside the network, allow 445 only to the file servers and domain controllers that need it, require SMB signing, and use SMB encryption for sensitive shares. Workstations rarely need to accept inbound SMB at all.

source.name: Microsoft Learn: Secure SMB traffic in Windows Server

title: Unique local administrator passwords (Windows LAPS)
guidance: A shared local administrator password lets one compromised machine unlock all the others. Windows LAPS gives every device a unique, rotating local admin password stored in Active Directory or Microsoft Entra ID, readable only by authorised staff. Combine it with restricting who may log on remotely as a local administrator.

title: Hardening the OpenSSH server
guidance: In sshd_config, prefer key-based authentication and set PasswordAuthentication no once keys work, set PermitRootLogin no (or prohibit-password if root access by key is required), and restrict who may log in with AllowUsers or AllowGroups. Keep OpenSSH updated. Validate the file with sshd -t and keep an existing session open while reloading, so a mistake cannot lock you out.

title: SSH exposed to the internet
guidance: An SSH port open to the whole internet is scanned and brute-forced constantly. Restrict it with the host or perimeter firewall to known administrator addresses, or put it behind a VPN or bastion host. Use keys rather than passwords, require MFA on the bastion where possible, and watch authentication logs for repeated failures.

source.name: MITRE ATT&CK T1133 External Remote Services

title: Remote Desktop (RDP) exposure
guidance: RDP on TCP 3389 exposed to the internet is a leading way into networks, through brute force and stolen credentials. Do not publish it directly: require a VPN or a Remote Desktop Gateway, enforce Network Level Authentication and MFA, limit the Remote Desktop Users group, and enable account lockout. Monitor for logons from unusual sources.

source.name: MITRE ATT&CK T1021.001 Remote Desktop Protocol

title: Securing remote access software
guidance: Remote monitoring and remote access tools (VNC, commercial remote desktop agents) give full control of a machine and are abused by attackers. Keep an inventory of approved tools, remove unapproved ones, keep them updated, require MFA, never leave them listening on the internet, and log every session.

source.name: CISA Guide to Securing Remote Access Software

title: Database ports must not face the internet
guidance: Database services (MySQL 3306, PostgreSQL 5432, SQL Server 1433, MongoDB 27017, Redis 6379) should listen only on internal interfaces and accept connections only from the application servers that need them. Bind to a private address, block the port at the firewall, require authentication with a strong unique password per application account, use TLS for connections, and give each application account only the privileges it needs.

title: Cleartext protocols: Telnet and FTP
guidance: Telnet and plain FTP send passwords and data unencrypted. Replace Telnet with SSH and FTP with SFTP or FTPS, then disable and remove the old service. If a legacy device only supports Telnet, restrict access to a management network and plan its replacement.

source.name: CIS Control 4: Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software

title: SNMP exposure
guidance: SNMP v1 and v2c authenticate with a community string sent in clear text, and default strings such as public and private are widely guessed. Use SNMPv3 with authentication and encryption, change any default community strings, allow SNMP only from the monitoring server, and block UDP 161 at the perimeter.

source.name: CISA: Reducing the Risk of SNMP Abuse

title: Apache httpd security tips
guidance: Keep Apache httpd and its modules updated, load only the modules you use, run the server as an unprivileged user, deny access to the filesystem by default and allow only the document directories, and disable directory listing (Options -Indexes) where it is not needed. Test configuration changes with apachectl configtest before a graceful reload.

title: Hiding the Apache version banner
guidance: ServerTokens Prod and ServerSignature Off stop Apache from advertising its exact version in headers and error pages. This removes easy fingerprinting but is not a fix: an outdated version is still vulnerable, so upgrade first and treat banner hiding as hygiene.

title: Configuring HTTPS on nginx
guidance: An nginx HTTPS server needs listen 443 ssl with ssl_certificate and ssl_certificate_key, and should restrict ssl_protocols to TLSv1.2 and TLSv1.3. Keep the private key readable only by root, redirect plain HTTP to HTTPS, and run nginx -t before nginx -s reload so a syntax error does not take the site down.

title: Hiding the nginx version
guidance: server_tokens off in the http block removes the nginx version from the Server header and error pages. As with any banner change, it reduces fingerprinting only; the real fix for a vulnerable version is upgrading nginx.

title: TLS configuration
guidance: Support only TLS 1.2 and 1.3, disable SSLv3, TLS 1.0 and 1.1, prefer modern cipher suites with forward secrecy, use certificates from a trusted CA with full chains, and renew before expiry. Enable HSTS once HTTPS works everywhere on the site. Re-test after changes with a TLS scanner.

source.name: OWASP Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet

title: Firewall policy: default deny
guidance: A firewall policy should deny traffic by default and allow only what a documented business need requires, by source, destination, port and protocol. Review rules regularly and remove ones nobody can justify. Separate networks of different trust levels, such as user workstations, servers and management interfaces.

source.name: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1: Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy

title: Changing firewall rules on a remote host without locking yourself out
guidance: Before changing a host firewall over the network, add the allow rule for your own management connection first, keep the current session open, and have out-of-band console access ready. Schedule an automatic revert (for example a timed job that restores the saved rules) and cancel it only after confirming access still works.

source.name: NIST SP 800-41 Rev. 1: Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy

title: ufw on Ubuntu
guidance: ufw is Ubuntu's front end to the kernel firewall. Allow SSH before enabling it (sudo ufw allow from <admin-network> to any port 22 proto tcp), set defaults with ufw default deny incoming and ufw default allow outgoing, then sudo ufw enable. Block a port with ufw deny <port>/tcp, list rules with ufw status numbered, and delete one with ufw delete <number>.

title: firewalld on RHEL
guidance: firewalld groups rules into zones. Check the active zone with firewall-cmd --get-active-zones, remove an unneeded service with firewall-cmd --zone=<zone> --remove-service=<service>, or allow a port only from a source with a rich rule. Changes without --permanent last until reload, which is a safe way to test; repeat with --permanent and run firewall-cmd --reload to keep them.

source.name: Red Hat: Configuring firewalls and packet filters

title: Remove or disable services you do not need
guidance: Every listening service is attack surface. Identify what listens (ss -tlnp on Linux, Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen on Windows), confirm with the owner whether it is needed, and uninstall or disable what is not. On Linux, systemctl disable --now <unit> stops it and keeps it from starting at boot; mask it if other units might start it. Confirm nothing depends on it before stopping a service on a production system.

source.name: CIS Control 4: Secure Configuration of Enterprise Assets and Software

title: Keep SELinux enforcing
guidance: SELinux confines services so a compromised process cannot reach files and ports outside its policy. If a service is blocked, read the denial with ausearch -m AVC or sealert and fix the label or boolean the denial points to, rather than running setenforce 0 or disabling SELinux. Permissive mode for a single domain is a narrower temporary option while a policy fix is prepared.

title: Account management and least privilege
guidance: Keep an inventory of user, administrator and service accounts; remove accounts that are no longer used; give each person and service only the privileges it needs; and use separate administrator accounts for administrative work. Service accounts should not have interactive logon rights unless they need them.

title: Keep audit logging on
guidance: Logs are how an intrusion is detected and investigated. Keep audit and system logging enabled, send logs to a central store the host cannot alter, keep them for a defined period, and review them. Stopping logging to save space or silence noise removes the evidence an investigation needs; tune what is collected instead.

title: Multi-factor authentication
guidance: MFA stops most attacks that rely on stolen or guessed passwords. Require it first for remote access (VPN, remote desktop gateways, email) and for administrator accounts, prefer phishing-resistant methods such as FIDO2 security keys, and keep a recovery process that does not bypass it.

title: Default and hard-coded credentials
guidance: Devices and software shipped with default passwords are trivially compromised once reachable. Change every default credential at installation, disable vendor accounts you do not use, and never embed passwords or keys in code or configuration committed to repositories; use a secrets store and rotate anything that was exposed.

source.name: MITRE CWE-1392: Use of Default Credentials

title: CWE Top 25 most dangerous weaknesses
guidance: The CWE Top 25 ranks the weakness types behind the most common and severe CVEs, such as cross-site scripting, out-of-bounds write, SQL injection, use after free, OS command injection, missing authorization and path traversal. When a CVE maps to one of these classes, the CWE entry describes the root cause and the mitigations developers should apply; for third-party software the practical fix is the vendor update.

title: Cross-site scripting (CWE-79)
guidance: XSS happens when untrusted input reaches a page without the right output encoding. Encode for the context (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript, URL), use frameworks that escape by default, sanitise any HTML you must accept with a vetted library, and add a Content Security Policy as a second layer. For a third-party application, apply the vendor fix.

source.name: OWASP Cross Site Scripting Prevention Cheat Sheet

title: SQL injection (CWE-89)
guidance: Use parameterised queries or prepared statements everywhere; never build SQL by concatenating input. Stored procedures and allow-list validation help, and the application's database account should have only the privileges it needs, so a successful injection cannot drop tables or read unrelated data.

source.name: OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet

title: Memory-safety flaws: out-of-bounds write (CWE-787) and similar
guidance: Out-of-bounds writes and use-after-free bugs in compiled software can lead to code execution and cannot be fixed by configuration. The remedy is the vendor's fixed version; until it is installed, reduce exposure by restricting network access to the affected service and keeping exploit mitigations such as ASLR and DEP enabled.

title: OS command injection (CWE-78)
guidance: Avoid calling a shell with user input. Use library functions instead of shell commands, pass arguments as a list rather than one string, and validate input against an allow-list. Run the process with the least privilege possible so an injection gains little.

source.name: OWASP OS Command Injection Defense Cheat Sheet

title: Path traversal (CWE-22)
guidance: Path traversal lets input like ../ reach files outside the intended directory. Map user choices to known file identifiers instead of using raw names, canonicalise the path and check it stays inside the allowed base directory, and run the service with file permissions that limit what it can read.

title: Missing authorization (CWE-862)
guidance: Every request that reads or changes data must check on the server that the caller is allowed to act on that specific object, not only that they are logged in. Deny by default, centralise the checks, and test with a second account that a user cannot reach another user's or tenant's records by changing an identifier.

title: Unsafe deserialization (CWE-502)
guidance: Deserializing untrusted data with native object formats can execute attacker code. Prefer simple data formats such as JSON with schema validation, never deserialize objects from untrusted sources, and where a library must be used, restrict the allowed classes and keep it updated.

title: Server-side request forgery (CWE-918)
guidance: SSRF makes a server fetch URLs an attacker chooses, often internal services or cloud metadata endpoints. Allow-list destination hosts and schemes, resolve and check the address before connecting, block private and link-local ranges, and do not return raw responses to the user.

title: Exploitation of public-facing applications (T1190)
guidance: Attackers exploit flaws in internet-facing software such as web servers, VPNs and edge devices to get in. Mitigations: keep exposed software patched first, isolate it in a DMZ with limited access inward, run it with least privilege, use a web application firewall where suitable, and scan the external attack surface regularly.

source.name: MITRE ATT&CK T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application

title: Brute force against exposed logins (T1110)
guidance: Password guessing and credential stuffing target exposed services such as SSH, RDP, VPNs and web logins. Mitigations: MFA, account lockout or rate limiting, strong password policy, removing direct internet exposure of administrative services, and alerting on bursts of failed logins.

title: Abuse of valid accounts (T1078)
guidance: Stolen or default credentials let attackers log in like real users and avoid many alerts. Mitigations: MFA, removing unused and default accounts, least privilege, privileged access management for administrators, and monitoring for logins at unusual times or from unusual places.

title: Exploitation of remote services (T1210)
guidance: Inside a network, attackers move between machines by exploiting vulnerable services such as SMB and RDP. Mitigations: patch internal services too, segment the network so workstations cannot reach every server, disable services that are not needed, and use exploit protection features.

source.name: MITRE ATT&CK T1210 Exploitation of Remote Services

title: Disabling security tools is an attack technique (T1562.001)
guidance: Turning off antivirus, EDR, firewalls or logging is exactly what attackers do to avoid detection (Impair Defenses). Legitimate troubleshooting should never require it: use narrow, documented exclusions, restrict who can change security settings, and alert when a security tool stops reporting.

source.name: MITRE ATT&CK T1562.001 Disable or Modify Tools

title: Update software (ATT&CK mitigation M1051)
guidance: Regularly updating software with patch management is the ATT&CK mitigation for many exploitation techniques. Prioritise externally reachable and widely used software, test updates on representative systems first, and confirm deployment across all assets, not only those with an agent.

title: OWASP Top 10 web application risks
guidance: The OWASP Top 10 lists the most critical web application risks, including broken access control, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, security misconfiguration, vulnerable and outdated components, and authentication failures. Use it to frame findings on web assets and to choose the matching OWASP cheat sheet for the fix.

title: Vulnerable and outdated components
guidance: Applications are often vulnerable through the libraries and frameworks they include. Keep an inventory of components and versions (an SBOM), remove unused dependencies, watch advisories for what you use, and upgrade to fixed versions promptly. A library fix usually needs the application to be rebuilt or redeployed, not only the host to be updated.

source.name: OWASP Top 10 A06:2021 Vulnerable and Outdated Components

title: Security misconfiguration
guidance: Misconfiguration covers default accounts, unnecessary features and ports, verbose error messages, missing security headers and permissive cloud storage. Use a repeatable hardened baseline for each platform, apply it automatically, and compare systems against it regularly to find drift.

title: Asset inventory (CIS Control 1)
guidance: You cannot protect what you do not know about. Keep an accurate inventory of every device connected to the network, including servers, workstations, network gear and IoT, using active and passive discovery. Investigate unknown devices, then either bring them under management or remove them.

source.name: CIS Control 1: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets

title: Software inventory (CIS Control 2)
guidance: Track the software installed on each asset, allow only authorised and supported software, and remove or isolate unsupported versions that no longer receive security fixes. A software inventory is what lets a new CVE be matched to the machines that actually run the affected version.

source.name: CIS Control 2: Inventory and Control of Software Assets

title: Continuous vulnerability management (CIS Control 7)
guidance: Scan assets regularly with authenticated scans where possible, remediate by risk on a documented schedule, and re-scan to confirm each fix. A finding should be closed only when a later scan or version check shows it is gone, not when the change ticket is closed.

title: Software bill of materials (SBOM)
guidance: An SBOM lists the components and versions inside a piece of software. It lets you answer quickly whether a newly published CVE affects you, and which assets to fix first. Keep SBOMs current as software is updated, and combine them with exploitability information from the supplier where available.

title: Security-focused configuration and change management
guidance: Changes to systems should be requested, analysed for security impact, approved, tested, implemented and verified, with a record of each step. Keep a secure baseline configuration for each system type, and compare systems against it so unapproved changes are noticed. Every change plan should say how to roll back.

title: Safe-change checklist before fixing a production system
guidance: Before a fix: confirm the asset owner agrees and a maintenance window is set, take a backup or snapshot, note the current version and configuration, test the change on a similar non-production system if one exists, and write down the rollback steps. After the fix: verify the service works, confirm the new version, re-scan, and record the result. Stop and roll back if verification fails.

title: Do not run downloaded scripts without checking them
guidance: Piping a downloaded script straight into a shell (curl ... | sh) runs whatever the server returns, with no integrity check. Install from the operating system's signed package repositories or the vendor's signed packages instead; when a script is unavoidable, download it, review it, and verify its checksum or signature before running it.

source.name: MITRE CWE-494: Download of Code Without Integrity Check

title: Overly permissive file permissions
guidance: Making files or directories world-writable (for example chmod 777) lets any local user or compromised service change them, which can lead to code execution or privilege escalation. Grant the specific owner or group only the access it needs, and fix the underlying ownership problem rather than opening permissions to everyone.

source.name: MITRE CWE-732: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource

title: Never turn off certificate verification
guidance: Disabling TLS certificate validation (for example curl -k, verify=False, or ignoring certificate errors) allows anyone on the network path to intercept and alter traffic. Fix the cause instead: install the right CA certificate in the trust store, correct the hostname, or renew the expired certificate.

title: If exploitation is suspected, treat it as an incident
guidance: If there are signs a vulnerability was already exploited, such as unknown accounts, unexpected processes or outbound connections, patching alone is not enough. Preserve evidence, contain the asset (for example isolate it from the network), involve the incident response team, and only then eradicate and recover. Rebuilding from a known-good image may be safer than cleaning in place.

source.name: NIST SP 800-61 Rev. 3: Incident Response Recommendations

title: Network devices and appliances need vendor fixes
guidance: Routers, firewalls, VPN gateways and other appliances are fixed by vendor firmware or software updates, not by host tools. Check the vendor advisory for the fixed release and any interim mitigations, back up the configuration before upgrading, schedule a window because upgrades often reboot the device, and restrict management interfaces to an internal management network. Edge devices with known exploited flaws should be patched first.

title: Inventory gaps: assets with no agent or no recent scan
guidance: An asset that has no agent or has not been scanned recently is a blind spot: its vulnerabilities and software are unknown, not absent. Find these gaps by comparing discovery sources, prioritise covering internet-facing and critical assets, and never read a missing scan as a clean result.

source.name: CIS Control 1: Inventory and Control of Enterprise Assets

title: Internet exposure review
guidance: Review which of your services can be reached from the internet and why. Each exposed port should have an owner and a business reason; remove the rest at the perimeter. Administrative interfaces, databases, file sharing and remote desktop should not be internet-facing. Re-check after network changes, because exposure often appears by accident.

source.name: MITRE ATT&CK T1133 External Remote Services

title: Broken access control
guidance: Broken access control is the top OWASP web risk: users acting outside their permissions, viewing other accounts' data by changing an ID, or reaching admin functions. Enforce checks on the server for every request, deny by default, log access-control failures, and rate-limit APIs.

source.name: OWASP Top 10 A01:2021 Broken Access Control
